Synopsis

Belgian ICS vendor eWON (later acquired by HMS Networks), which provides remote connectivity tools for industrial equipment, was targeted during the Dragonfly/Havex campaign attributed to Russia's FSB Center 16. Legitimate eWON installers such as the eCatcher VPN client were made available from the vendor site with Havex malware added. This record tracks the eWON product scope specifically; related Havex vendor compromises are tracked separately.

Story

Dragonfly, also called Energetic Bear, Crouching Yeti, and Berzerk Bear, did not need to invent a new trust path into industrial networks. It used the one engineers already followed. During the Havex phase, the operators compromised ICS and SCADA software providers and placed malware inside legitimate vendor downloads.

eWON was one of the public vendor scopes tied to that activity. Its remote-access tooling, including eCatcher-style VPN software used to reach industrial equipment, was a valuable bridge between ordinary workstations and operational environments. A poisoned installer from the official vendor site could enter a plant as maintenance software, not as an obvious intrusion.

Havex gave the operators a backdoor, contacted command infrastructure, gathered host and credential information, and could deploy an OPC scanning component to look for industrial control devices. The DOJ indictment says the broader campaign put malware on more than 17,000 unique devices in the United States and elsewhere, including systems tied to power and energy operations.

This record keeps the eWON artifacts separate from the other Havex vendor compromises because the package scope is different even when the actor and campaign are the same. The dates here describe the public trojanized-download window reported for this vendor scope; the indictment describes related supplier intrusions beginning earlier.
